/society/2026/nov/15/no-free-lunch-milbu.headline: Burnham unveils guaranteed jobs and childhood-level support for young people
/society/2026/nov/15/no-free-lunch-milbu.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools.

Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”.

He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade.

Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer, Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”.

“If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham.

Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

Instead of personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, some young people will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit.

The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year.

Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it.

Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront.

Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.”

Pat McFadden acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently.

The work and pensions secretary said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work.

But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said.

“You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work.

McFadden said the change was necessary because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%.

Burnham criticised the Conservatives and Reform for calling for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, pointing to Kemi Badenoch’s vow to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election.

Labour called the Conservatives’ proposals “a charter for human misery”, arguing the plans would cut 70% of child benefit disability-related claims linked to ADHD and “milder” behavioural disorders and learning disabilities.

The shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, acknowledged the plans could mean around half a million children losing disability-related payments.

“This is to help those children,” she told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, adding that under the plans, child mental health services would receive £1bn of funding. “The point of that funding is because there are children who are struggling. Let’s use this funding in the best possible way to support those children.”

Burnham said past Conservative governments had taken “a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt” of austerity cuts. “What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again,” he said.

“The crude cuts they are proposing … would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.”

A survey of young people by the Children’s Commissioner, which received more than 1 million responses, found that more than half were worried about getting a good job in the future.

Young people want to work, the responses revealed, though they face “huge challenges” finding experience and opportunities, said Dame Rachel de Souza.

“The message is clear. Young people are ambitious, they want to work, they want a good job,” she said.

“We need to help them get the skills, the experience and opportunities to find work.

“They need a full, rich education that gives them the knowledge and skills to get on in life, but too many are being let down by the advice and careers support they receive, which many young people do not feel isn’t good enough.”

Responding to the survey, Milburn said he had not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet while writing the review.

“All too often the system – from health to welfare to the labour market – has failed them. That’s why a fundamental system reset is needed to give hope back to young people,” he said.

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: Campaigners hail ‘historic day’ as pardon clears abortion convictions
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.bodyHtml:
Campaigners and women previously convicted of illegal abortions have hailed a “historic day” as every woman who has faced criminal investigation for ending a pregnancy over the last 150 years is pardoned.

A vote in the House of Lords earlier this year introduced legislation to pardon women accused of terminating their own pregnancies outside the legal framework and expunge their criminal records, under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which takes effect on Monday.

The House of Commons had previously voted to amend the laws around abortion to prevent future cases of women being criminalised for ending their own pregnancies, while keeping the legal framework for terminations in place.

Some women have said that while they are “grateful” for the pardon, they would also like a formal apology from the government, as “none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison”.

It is understood that the pardons will apply to about 150 women, who have been identified from police records.

Details of convictions, cautions, arrests and police investigations relating to terminations will now be deleted from the women’s records, allowing them to work and travel without restrictions once more.

Several women faced prosecution after ordering medication online or obtaining drugs following a remote consultation, including during the Covid-19 pandemic, to terminate their pregnancies.

Nicola Packer is among those who have spoken publicly about not realising they were beyond 24 weeks at the time; she was cleared by a jury at Isleworth crown court in London last year after an almost five-year ordeal.

She was prosecuted after she obtained pills from an authorised provider at the height of the pandemic, and had not realised that her pregnancy was more advanced than she initially thought.

Laura*, a young mother who was jailed after her abusive partner coerced her into obtaining pills online, is among the women who have advocated for a change in the law after experiencing domestic abuse or coercive control.

“We’ve all been through so much to get here,” Packer said. “Although it can’t erase the memories of what we’ve experienced, it does remove the records that have made it difficult for some of us to get and keep jobs, and live our lives.”

“And it further validates the feeling that none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison,” she added. “It’s a great day for us and I feel lighter knowing that the records have been expunged.”

Amy* said she was “grateful” for the pardon, though it did not “undo the years of stigma, distress and judgment”. She said women had their parenting questioned, faced restrictions on contact with their own children and were seen as “a serious danger to society”.

“I do believe women deserved an apology for what they went through,” she said. “Although the authorities may have been acting within the law at the time, we have to remember that for many women, particularly during Covid, there was isolation, fear and nowhere to turn.

“Women were dealing with incredibly difficult circumstances, often without the support or help they needed.”

She added: “For me, the hardest part is knowing that I will always carry this experience with me. The publicity surrounding my case meant that my identity and where I lived became public knowledge.

“People know who I am and where I live, and even now I can struggle to walk into my local community without feeling that people are looking at me or judging me. Having a pardon doesn’t take away those experiences or give me back the privacy I lost.”

Up until the recent law change, women were often prosecuted under Victorian legislation dating back to 1861. They include Fanny Warboys, who was criminalised a year later, in 1862, a widow who ended up injured after a backstreet abortion and was sentenced to three months in prison.

Another woman, Mary Jane Baynon, 32, was jailed for three months in 1891 after travelling to London from her home in Sligo in western Ireland, and being reported to police by a fake surgeon.

In an early example of judges showing compassion for women who found themselves before the courts, Emma Sarah Rice, 25, was found guilty of an illegal abortion, but was sentenced to just one day without hard labour in 1881. She was still pregnant and in ill health, and “his Lordship said he thought the woman was more to be pitied than condemned”.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said the pardons recognised “the injustice of historical convictions” and she was “delighted to see this progress”.

Dr Jonathan Lord, the co-chair of the RCOG’s abortion taskforce, welcomed a “historic day”, when “for the first time since the 13th century, women who have been convicted after a pregnancy loss for an alleged abortion will no longer have to carry the consequences of a criminal record”.

Many of the women prosecuted had no other convictions or cautions, but found themselves unable to work in certain jobs because they had been arrested for abortion offences.

Others found themselves having to disclose traumatic medical events to potential employers, even though they were never charged with a crime, as their arrests had shown on enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service checks.

Heidi Stewart, the chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS), said: “For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws … While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

Women affected do not need to apply to have their convictions removed, or take any action, as police forces and courts will begin updating records in line with new requirements, which the government has described as “a priority”.

Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, said: “Pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy has been a priority and I’m pleased to be able to commence the change that parliament voted for.

“For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team.”

*Names have been changed

/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.headline: More than 165,000 back Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.bodyHtml:
Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 165,000 people who have signed an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.

The letter calls on the company's board members to 'bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts'.

Huang's resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations that he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

US lawmakers from both parties are pressing Huang and Nvidia to appear before Congress and explain whether US national security was put at risk, with some in the president's own party saying Donald Trump's administration must also answer questions on what it knew about Huang's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him, with one ally telling the paper they were putting together a 'war room' of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House.

'Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,' the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang's support.

Two major shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board on Friday to keep 'all options' open.

In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look 'outside' the company for its next chief, telling Fox News: 'They need a dramatic shake-up.'

Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it had knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this mattered more than Huang's affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.

The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.

'Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,' Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine 'whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions'.

Bessent said he wanted answers within the next 10 days from Nvidia and its internal investigation into Jensen Huang's behaviour.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang's return include Tim Sweeney, founder and chief executive of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, the Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had 'erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company'.

More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18 per cent of the company's workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname 'the central bank of AI'.

The company has also faced criticism, however, that it fuelled a speculative investment bubble, with Huang fighting any constraints on the AI race and clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief, Dario Amodei.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, officials said, though no date has yet been set.

/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.headline: F1 renews diversity funding as Hamilton calls for faster progress
/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.bodyHtml:
Lewis Hamilton has urged Formula One to push harder and move faster on diversity and inclusion, warning that the future of the sport depends on taking robust action to address inequality in recruitment.

Hamilton has called on F1 to make greater investment, more extensive recording and publishing of data on who is in the sport, and a commitment from teams to guarantee a number of paid early-career places for young people from underrepresented backgrounds.

Hamilton’s Mission 44 foundation, established in 2021, has published a new report, titled Igniting Inclusion, five years after the groundbreaking assessment made by the Hamilton commission to investigate and address the lack of representation of black people, women and those from lower‑income backgrounds in motorsport.

The new review shows F1 still has much work to do, the seven‑time world champion insists.

‘Formula One is inspiring millions of young people around the world but inspiration means nothing without opportunity,’ Hamilton said. ‘We can’t tell young people to dream big and then not open the doors when they try to make those dreams a reality.

‘F1, the FIA and every team must push harder and move faster. We need real investment, more opportunities and greater accountability. We’ve shown that change is possible. Now we need to go further. The talent is out there, and the future of our sport depends on unlocking it.’

Hamilton pointed to progress made since 2021, including a diversity and inclusion charter now signed by the FIA, Formula One and all 11 teams.

F1 has also published a social impact report showing that it has renewed its engineering scholarships with a three-year commitment of £2.4m of funding, and that more than 500,000 young people from 71 countries have used its educational programmes. The all‑female F1 Academy is now also a key part of the sport.

The new report was nonetheless critical, noting that F1 still did not keep records of whether the make-up of the sport was changing – specifically, whether more people from underrepresented groups are reaching careers in F1 than in 2021.

Igniting Inclusion calls for three areas to be addressed. First, a yearly submission by teams, F1 and the FIA of who enters and leaves and is promoted within the sport, by gender, ethnicity and socioeconomic background; this would be delivered to an independent data partner that would publish one sport-wide picture. Second, for the same parties to invest £50m over five years to help young people from underrepresented backgrounds into the sport, with those new roles excluded from the cost cap. Third, a commitment by teams to provide a published number of paid, accessible, early-career places each year.

Hamilton said F1 risked missing out on a new generation of talent if it did not act decisively: ‘Five years ago, I launched the Hamilton Commission because I knew Formula One had to change. Since then, we’ve worked tirelessly to break down barriers and open doors. We’ve helped drive real progress. I’m proud of what we’ve achieved, but we’re nowhere near finished.’

The new report included polling commissioned from 3,000 fans across the UK, US and Brazil, which found strong demand for F1 to act: 80 per cent of those polled believed greater representation would help F1 attract fans and sponsors, while 64 per cent thought F1’s leadership should be doing more to improve inclusion.

Since the original Hamilton report, Hamilton has invested £20m in the Mission 44 project. The foundation supports schoolchildren facing poverty and a lack of role models, encouraging them to pursue science, technology, engineering or maths (Stem) skills and careers in motorsport.

In partnership with the Royal Academy of Engineering, it has been meeting the costs of scholars studying for a master’s degree in motorsport engineering, open to 12 students of black or mixed black heritage, women and those from lower-income backgrounds regardless of ethnicity.

/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.headline: Russell Brand accuser Mia Latter waives anonymity to call for consent law change
/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.bodyHtml:
A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent.

Mia Latter says she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16.

Previously identified using the pseudonym “Alice”, Latter said in an interview with the Sunday Times that she had been inspired by Gisèle Pelicot to give up her lifelong right to anonymity. “It’s not my shame,” she said. “It’s not my burden to carry any more. It’s not me lying, and I didn’t commit any crimes.”

Latter is calling on the UK government to introduce a “staggered” consent law, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said that Latter’s “heartbreaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.

She told the Sunday Times: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.

“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”

Under UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with consenting 16- and 17-year-olds.

Latter told the paper: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about [Brand], it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.

“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

Latter, now 37, was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip. He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.

She said that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had told him her age.

Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship. Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.

Latter spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court.

Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

The Metropolitan police are looking at a series of “serious” sexual offence allegations against the comedian David Walliams, it was announced earlier this week, following an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’ accusers was asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.

“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”

It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.

Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.

“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”

Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She said it was “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”

The Met police said their investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing, after Latter’s allegation was reported to them. A spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.headline: Prince Harry vows to help Ukraine host future Invictus Games
/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.bodyHtml:
Prince Harry travelled to Ukraine on a surprise visit and told its soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia.

The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, where he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had felt ‘warmth’ when arriving in the country on Saturday, despite the risk involved in travelling there.

The British army veteran has now visited Ukraine four times since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.

He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in the care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.

He said: ‘Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.’

Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham, its largest ever team, and Harry watched wheelchair rugby players hoping to be among them.

The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. ‘When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,’ he promised.

At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was ‘still an active serviceman’, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.

Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport ‘all started and continues with the Invictus Games’.

The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine ‘a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank’ and said ‘it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that’.

The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.headline: Rambert turns It’s a Sin into a dance piece rooted in club joy
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.bodyHtml:
Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. The series follows young gay friends finding friendship amid the Aids crisis in 1980s London.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance, he said, felt different: “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which marked its centenary this year with a commitment to reaching new audiences, partly by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders. “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin.

Davies has a cameo in the trailer. His own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”), but the dancefloor has always been an inspiration to him. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.”

Pouffer has seen the dance world’s losses from the Aids epidemic first-hand. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” he said. Dancing in the US in the mid-90s, he saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?”

Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. Video and narration, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly, will help tell the story. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur.

Davies was turned down by all the major UK networks when he originally pitched the TV series, before Channel 4 eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said.

The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”.

There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’”

  • It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027
